altText: Navy slide with Educate Me AI logo. Text: Your 2027 GCSE Chemistry exam dates. Chemistry and Combined Science. AQA, Edexcel and OCR. Save this.

Two date cards: Chemistry paper 1, Monday 17 May, morning. Chemistry paper 2, Tuesday 15 June, morning. Same dates for Chemistry and Combined Science (AQA Trilogy, Edexcel, OCR Gateway). Paper numbers vary by board. Foundation and Higher are on the same day.

How long is each paper? Chemistry on all three boards: 1 hour 45 minutes each. Combined Science, AQA Trilogy: 1 hour 15 minutes each. Combined Science, Edexcel: 1 hour 10 minutes each. Combined Science, OCR Gateway: 1 hour 10 minutes each. On AQA Synergy or OCR Combined Science B, papers are split differently, so check your board's timetable.

A simple plan from now to May. 1: Now to Christmas, do one practice paper and note which topics cost the most marks. 2: January to Easter, one topic a week plus a few calculation questions every week. 3: Easter to May, timed papers, Paper 1 topics first, then Paper 2.

Before each paper. Questions on the practicals you did in class come up in the written papers, so know the method and why each step matters. In calculations, write down each step with units and check the answer looks sensible. Learn which topics are on Paper 1 and Paper 2 for your board.
Navy end slide with Em’s three circles in green, orange and pink. Text: Save this. Send it to your Chemistry group. Follow for a new revision plan every week.

posts.title: Why does a raw potato chip go floppy in salty water?
posts.planGate: Metricool Free plan: schedule only after Rej has confirmed the Starter upgrade in chat
altText: Reel, Lock It In number 1, GCSE Biology, Combined and Triple Science. Question: why does a raw potato chip go floppy in salty water? A diagram shows a potato cell on the left and salty water on the right, separated by a dashed cell membrane. Water dots move across the membrane into the salty water and the cell shrinks. Text: Osmosis: water crosses a partially permeable membrane, from dilute to more concentrated. Salty water is more concentrated, so water leaves the potato cells. So the chip goes floppy and loses mass. Memory trick: water follows the salt. In pure water it's the other way round: water moves in and the chip goes firm. Ends on: Save this. Lock it in. Follow for Lock It In number 2.

platforms.label: Instagram Reel
platforms.caption:
Why does a raw potato chip go floppy in salty water? Osmosis. Water moves across a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one, so water leaves the potato cells and the chip loses mass.

Memory trick: water follows the salt. In pure water it goes the other way, and the chip goes firm.

posts.title: Wrong answer. Still marks?
posts.planGate: Metricool Free plan: schedule only after Rej has confirmed the Starter upgrade in chat
altText: Short video with on-screen captions. Opens with the title 'Wrong answer. Still marks?' while the question appears behind it. The question 'A coat costs £80. In a sale it's 15% off. What is the sale price?' is worked line by line. The first two lines, 10% = £8 so 5% = £4, and 15% = £8 + £4 = £12, together get a green 'Method ✓' and the mark counter rises to 1 out of 3. The last line, £80 − £12 = £58, gets a green 'Method ✓', taking the counter to 2, and a pink 'Answer ✗'. A note says it should be £68. The counter stays at 2. Ends with 'Show every step.' and the Educate Me AI logo.

platforms.label: Instagram Reel
platforms.caption:
A wrong final answer doesn't always mean zero. If your working is on the page, correct method can still pick up marks.

Here, finding 15% (£12) earns a method mark, and subtracting it from £80 earns another. The subtraction slips (£58, not £68), so only the answer mark is lost: 2 of the 3 example marks. With just '£58' written down, there'd be nothing to give marks for.

Save this for your next practice paper.
